title: Procedural due process: protected interests and adequate procedure
shortTitle: Procedural due process: protected interests and adequate procedure
summary: A due-process claim asks first whether government deprives a protected life, liberty, or property interest, then which procedures and timing the Constitution requires.
notes:
Procedural due process constrains governmental deprivation of life, liberty, or property under the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments. Roth and Perry distinguish the threshold existence of a protected interest from the adequacy of procedures. Once that threshold is met, timing matters as much as format: a later evidentiary hearing may or may not sufficiently protect against an interim loss. The APA and organic statutes can provide protections beyond the constitutional minimum.

Henry Friendly’s inventory identifies potential safeguards including an impartial decisionmaker, notice of grounds, a chance to respond and present witnesses, access to adverse evidence, a record-based decision, representation, reasons, public attendance, and review. The inventory is a set of possible ingredients, not a requirement that every administrative decision contain all eleven. Mathews assesses private interests, the risk of error and likely value of additional safeguards, and government interests and burdens.

The editors compare three sources of justification. Tradition can guide procedural judgment but requires selecting among competing historical analogies. Dignity and autonomy explain why participation matters independently of accuracy, but leave difficult questions about limiting principles. Interest balancing adapts to different programs yet demands information and comparisons that may be hard to obtain. The reading attributes these concerns to scholars and the editors rather than presenting them as a single controlling judicial formula. The historical discussion also links the volume of due-process litigation to changes in governmental activity and the institutions implementing public programs.
